item.content:encoded:
The D-Prize Competition 2026 is now open for entrepreneurs, innovators and changemakers who want to launch new organizations that distribute proven solutions to poverty. The competition provides seed funding of up to US$20,000 to selected applicants seeking to expand access to interventions that can improve lives in underserved communities.

D-Prize is built around a simple but important development challenge: many effective poverty solutions already exist, but they do not reach enough people who need them. The competition supports entrepreneurs who can build organizations focused on the distribution, delivery and scaling of evidence-based solutions.

Rather than funding the invention of entirely new products, D-Prize prioritizes ideas that can help deliver existing, proven interventions to people living in poverty. Successful applicants are expected to launch a pilot, demonstrate that their distribution model works and build an organization capable of expanding its impact.

The Global Competition launches on 14 September 2026. Applicants can submit their proposals through the early, regular or extension submission deadlines.

What Is the D-Prize Competition?

D-Prize is a global competition that supports entrepreneurs who want to establish organizations dedicated to distributing proven poverty solutions.

The programme is based on the principle that development interventions can have a greater impact when they are effectively delivered to communities that lack access to them. These interventions may already be supported by research and evidence, but distribution challenges can prevent them from reaching the last mile.

D-Prize seeks entrepreneurs who can answer a central question:

How can an existing, evidence-based poverty solution be distributed more effectively to people who need it most?

Selected entrepreneurs receive seed funding to launch a new organization, test their distribution model and begin building a scalable operation.

The competition focuses on the practical delivery of solutions rather than simply identifying social problems. Applicants must demonstrate how their proposed organization will move a proven intervention from existing supply channels to underserved populations.

How the D-Prize Model Works

The D-Prize model is structured around three main stages:

1. Identify a Proven Poverty Solution

Applicants select an intervention from the D-Prize challenge list or propose another evidence-based intervention that is not currently listed.

The intervention should have credible evidence demonstrating that it can improve outcomes related to poverty, health, education, agriculture, livelihoods, water, public services or other development priorities.

2. Build a Distribution Organization

Applicants develop a plan for launching an organization that will distribute the selected intervention to underserved communities.

The proposed organization may focus on activities such as:

  • Delivering products to hard-to-reach communities.
  • Connecting vulnerable populations with existing services.
  • Improving access to essential health interventions.
  • Supporting farmers with proven agricultural inputs or services.
  • Expanding access to education and learning interventions.
  • Connecting low-income households with public services.
  • Providing information, training or support that improves access to proven solutions.

3. Pilot and Scale the Organization

Selected entrepreneurs use the seed funding to launch a pilot and test whether their distribution model works.

After demonstrating initial results, entrepreneurs are expected to raise additional funding and expand their organizations to reach thousands or potentially millions of people.

D-Prize therefore seeks applicants who are not only passionate about social impact but also capable of building practical, sustainable and scalable organizations.

D-Prize Funding: Up to US$20,000

Selected entrepreneurs can receive up to US$20,000 in seed funding to launch a new organization distributing a proven poverty solution.

The funding is intended to help applicants move from an idea to early implementation. Depending on the proposed intervention and operating model, the award may support activities such as:

  • Initial programme implementation.
  • Distribution of products or services.
  • Community outreach.
  • Recruitment and training.
  • Pilot operations.
  • Monitoring and evaluation.
  • Local partnerships.
  • Transportation and logistics.
  • Early organizational expenses.
  • Testing and refining the distribution model.

Applicants should explain how the funding will be used to launch and test their organization. The award is designed as seed capital rather than long-term operational funding.

Entrepreneurs are expected to use the pilot stage to generate evidence, demonstrate effectiveness and position their organization for future fundraising and growth.

Who Is D-Prize Looking For?

D-Prize is particularly interested in entrepreneurs who want to establish new organizations focused on distributing evidence-based poverty interventions.

Most awardees are described as first-time entrepreneurs who have not yet launched an organization or raised significant outside funding. Applicants do not necessarily need to have an established nonprofit, company or extensive organizational history.

The competition is especially encouraging applicants from low- and middle-income countries, where distribution gaps may prevent proven poverty solutions from reaching vulnerable populations.

Potential applicants may include:

  • Social entrepreneurs.
  • Development practitioners.
  • Public health innovators.
  • Education entrepreneurs.
  • Agricultural entrepreneurs.
  • Community organizers.
  • Researchers interested in implementation.
  • Nonprofit founders.
  • Youth-led social impact teams.
  • Early-stage innovators.
  • Professionals seeking to launch a poverty-focused organization.

The key requirement is not simply having a good idea. Applicants must propose a credible plan to distribute a proven intervention and demonstrate the potential to reach people living in poverty.

Eligibility Requirements

D-Prize prioritizes new organizations and early-stage entrepreneurs.

New Organizations

The competition is primarily designed for applicants who have not yet launched an organization or who are still at the earliest stage of development.

Most awardees are first-time entrepreneurs who:

  • Have not yet launched their proposed organization.
  • Have not raised substantial outside funding.
  • Are developing a new distribution-focused organization.
  • Want to test and scale a proven poverty solution.

Existing Organizations

Existing organizations may be considered, but only under specific conditions.

An existing organization may be eligible if its core focus is distributing an existing, evidence-based poverty intervention.

However, organizations with:

  • More than 18 months of full-time operations, or
  • More than US$30,000 raised,

are typically not supported.

Applicants with established organizations should carefully review the official eligibility guidance and frequently asked questions before applying.

Geographic Encouragement

D-Prize especially encourages applications from entrepreneurs based in low- and middle-income countries.

The supplied competition information does not state that applicants must be citizens of a particular country or continent. However, the programme’s emphasis is on poverty-focused distribution models that can serve underserved populations, particularly in low-resource settings.

Applicants should confirm any additional geographic or operational requirements in the official application materials.

D-Prize Intervention Areas

Applicants can choose from several intervention categories. These challenges cover a broad range of sectors connected to poverty reduction, health, education, agriculture, livelihoods and public services.

The listed categories include:

  • Agriculture.
  • Custom interventions.
  • DMPA-SC.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Livelihoods.
  • Public services.
  • Water.

Each intervention page provides a specific challenge question and an application packet that explains the problem, the intervention and the distribution opportunity.

Available D-Prize Challenges

The D-Prize website lists multiple intervention challenges. Applicants should review the available options and select an intervention that matches their interests, skills, local context and distribution capacity.

1. Childhood Diarrhea Treatment

This challenge focuses on distributing oral rehydration salts, commonly known as ORS, and zinc to households before children become sick.

Childhood diarrhea remains a serious threat to children under five, particularly where families lack timely access to treatment. The challenge asks entrepreneurs to develop a distribution model that helps ensure households can access ORS and zinc when needed.

Potential distribution approaches may involve:

  • Community health workers.
  • Pharmacies and local retailers.
  • Health facilities.
  • Household education.
  • Community-based distribution.
  • Partnerships with health organizations.

Applicants should review the official challenge packet for the specific intervention and evidence requirements.

2. DMPA-SC: Reaching Underserved Populations

This challenge focuses on distributing DMPA-SC, a self-injectable contraceptive method, to underserved populations.

The goal is to improve access to reproductive health services and ensure that people who face barriers to conventional healthcare delivery can access appropriate contraceptive options.

Applicants may consider distribution models involving:

  • Community-based providers.
  • Health facilities.
  • Outreach programmes.
  • Local health networks.
  • Training and referral systems.
  • Supply-chain partnerships.

Any proposed model must comply with applicable health regulations and clinical requirements.

3. DMPA-SC: Improving Provider Training

This intervention focuses on improving mandatory provider training for DMPA-SC.

The challenge asks entrepreneurs to develop ways to strengthen the training, knowledge and preparedness of providers responsible for delivering DMPA-SC services.

Potential activities may include:

  • Improving training delivery.
  • Expanding access to provider education.
  • Developing training-support systems.
  • Strengthening assessment and supervision.
  • Improving training completion and quality assurance.

Applicants should consult the official challenge materials for the required training standards and implementation expectations.

4. DMPA-SC: Last-Mile Inventory Management

This challenge focuses on improving the management of DMPA-SC supplies at the last mile.

Weak inventory management can lead to stockouts, wastage, delays and limited access to essential health products. Applicants are encouraged to develop distribution solutions that improve visibility, availability and management of supplies.

Possible areas of focus include:

  • Inventory tracking.
  • Stock monitoring.
  • Demand forecasting.
  • Supply-chain coordination.
  • Reporting systems.
  • Distribution planning.
  • Stockout prevention.

5. DMPA-SC: Medical Waste Management

This challenge asks entrepreneurs to improve the safe disposal of DMPA-SC needles.

The intervention focuses on reducing risks associated with medical waste and improving the safe handling and disposal of used injection equipment.

Applicants may explore solutions involving:

  • Safe collection systems.
  • Disposal partnerships.
  • Provider training.
  • Community awareness.
  • Waste tracking.
  • Appropriate disposal infrastructure.

All proposed approaches must follow relevant public health and medical waste regulations.

6. Reading Glasses

This challenge focuses on distributing non-prescription reading or working glasses to people who need them.

Many individuals experience difficulty reading or performing close-up tasks but may not have access to affordable vision support. The challenge asks entrepreneurs to develop a distribution model that can make suitable reading glasses more accessible.

Potential target groups may include:

  • Older adults.
  • Workers who require close-up vision.
  • Low-income households.
  • Rural communities.
  • People with limited access to optical services.

Applicants should ensure that their proposed model includes appropriate screening, product quality and referral pathways where necessary.

7. Childcare

The childcare challenge focuses on helping low-income families access quality childcare services.

Affordable and reliable childcare can support children’s development while enabling parents and caregivers to work, study or participate in economic activities.

Applicants may consider distribution or access models involving:

  • Community childcare networks.
  • Childcare referrals.
  • Local service providers.
  • Subsidized access systems.
  • Parent information platforms.
  • Partnerships with existing childcare organizations.

8. ConnectEd Phone-Based Tutoring

This education challenge focuses on distributing a phone-based intervention designed to improve learning outcomes.

The model may be particularly relevant in areas where students have limited access to formal tutoring, educational technology or qualified teachers.

Applicants may explore ways to deliver phone-based learning support through:

  • Mobile phones.
  • Voice calls.
  • SMS-based systems.
  • Local education partnerships.
  • Teacher or tutor networks.
  • Community learning programmes.

The specific intervention requirements should be reviewed in the official challenge packet.

9. Teaching at the Right Level

This challenge focuses on improving foundational literacy and numeracy in resource-limited classrooms.

Teaching at the Right Level is an approach that organizes instruction according to students’ actual learning levels rather than only their age or grade.

Applicants may develop distribution models that help schools and education systems access:

  • Teacher training.
  • Instructional materials.
  • Assessment tools.
  • Classroom support.
  • Implementation guidance.
  • Monitoring systems.

The goal is to help children develop foundational reading, writing and numeracy skills.

10. Road Safety

The road safety challenge focuses on replicating a proven public transport safety campaign to reduce road deaths.

Applicants are expected to identify ways to distribute or implement evidence-based road safety messaging and practices among transport operators, passengers, communities or other relevant groups.

Potential approaches may include:

  • Driver education.
  • Passenger awareness.
  • Public transport partnerships.
  • Community campaigns.
  • Safety communication.
  • Behaviour-change initiatives.

11. Government Transparency

This challenge focuses on monitoring and reporting data to reduce corruption and improve public service delivery.

Applicants may develop organizations that help communities, civil society groups or public institutions collect, analyze and use information to strengthen accountability.

Potential areas of work include:

  • Public service monitoring.
  • Community reporting.
  • Data collection.
  • Transparency platforms.
  • Citizen feedback.
  • Public expenditure tracking.
  • Accountability mechanisms.

12. Poverty Graduation

The poverty graduation challenge focuses on providing coaching, capital and social support to help people move out of extreme poverty.

A graduation approach typically combines several forms of support, which may include:

  • Livelihood assistance.
  • Business or income-generation support.
  • Coaching.
  • Financial services.
  • Skills development.
  • Social protection.
  • Community support.

Applicants should review the challenge packet to understand the specific intervention and evidence base expected by D-Prize.

13. Agriculture: Propose Your Own

Applicants can propose the distribution of an evidence-based agricultural intervention that is not already included on the D-Prize challenge list.

The proposed intervention should have credible evidence and address a clear agricultural or rural development need.

Potential areas could include:

  • Improved agricultural practices.
  • Farmer training.
  • Quality inputs.
  • Market access.
  • Climate-smart agriculture.
  • Livestock services.
  • Agricultural technologies.
  • Soil improvement.
  • Smallholder productivity.

Applicants must demonstrate why the intervention is evidence-based and explain how their organization will distribute it effectively.

14. Post-Harvest Support

This challenge focuses on providing smallholder farmers with post-harvest loans and storage technologies that have been shown to be effective.

Post-harvest losses can reduce farmer income, food availability and market stability. The challenge encourages distribution models that help farmers preserve, store or finance agricultural produce after harvest.

Potential components may include:

  • Storage technologies.
  • Post-harvest financing.
  • Farmer training.
  • Market linkages.
  • Warehouse partnerships.
  • Loss-reduction services.

15. Quality Agricultural Inputs

This challenge focuses on providing smallholder farmers with quality agricultural inputs and training to increase harvests.

Applicants may explore ways to improve access to:

  • Quality seeds.
  • Fertilizers.
  • Agricultural tools.
  • Crop protection products.
  • Farmer training.
  • Extension services.
  • Input distribution networks.

The proposed model should prioritize affordability, quality assurance and effective access for smallholder farmers.

16. Water Filters

This challenge focuses on distributing ceramic water filters to people living in areas without reliable access to clean water.

Applicants are expected to develop a distribution model that makes water filtration technology accessible to underserved households.

Potential activities may include:

  • Community distribution.
  • Household education.
  • Retail partnerships.
  • Installation and maintenance support.
  • Water, sanitation and hygiene awareness.
  • Monitoring of filter use.

17. Kangaroo Care

This health challenge focuses on improving access to Kangaroo Care, a proven but underused intervention for infants born too soon or too small.

Kangaroo Care involves practices that support the care and development of vulnerable newborns, including skin-to-skin contact and related supportive care approaches.

Applicants may explore distribution and awareness models involving:

  • Hospitals.
  • Maternity facilities.
  • Midwives.
  • Community health workers.
  • Parent education.
  • Newborn-care networks.

18. Oxygen

This challenge focuses on developing a team of technicians who can service and repair existing oxygen concentrators.

Medical oxygen is essential for treating several serious health conditions, but equipment failures can limit access in health facilities. The challenge asks entrepreneurs to improve the maintenance and availability of oxygen concentrators.

Potential activities may include:

  • Training technicians.
  • Establishing repair networks.
  • Providing maintenance services.
  • Supporting health facilities.
  • Managing spare parts.
  • Developing equipment-monitoring systems.

19. Patient Identification

This challenge focuses on identifying patients who need treatment for conditions such as:

  • Obstetric fistula.
  • Cervical cancer.
  • Clubfoot.
  • Cataracts.

The proposed organization would then connect identified patients with existing treatment services in their area.

Possible activities may include:

  • Community screening and awareness.
  • Patient referral systems.
  • Health-worker partnerships.
  • Case identification.
  • Transport coordination.
  • Treatment navigation.
  • Follow-up support.

20. Maternal Health

This challenge focuses on training birth attendants to administer misoprostol to help prevent maternal deaths caused by postpartum hemorrhage.

Applicants may explore distribution models involving:

  • Birth attendants.
  • Community health workers.
  • Maternal health organizations.
  • Training programmes.
  • Health facilities.
  • Referral networks.

Because this intervention involves medication and maternal healthcare, applicants must follow national clinical, regulatory and public health requirements.

21. Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission

This challenge focuses on counselling and motivating HIV-positive pregnant women to adhere to antiretroviral therapy and reduce the risk of mother-to-child HIV transmission.

Potential distribution models may involve:

  • Community health workers.
  • Maternal health clinics.
  • HIV support networks.
  • Patient counselling.
  • Treatment adherence systems.
  • Referral and follow-up services.

22. Child Immunization

This challenge focuses on directing caregivers to bring children to health facilities for routine immunizations that might otherwise be missed.

Applicants may develop systems involving:

  • Community mobilization.
  • Reminder services.
  • Health-worker outreach.
  • Parent education.
  • Immunization tracking.
  • Referral and follow-up.
  • Partnerships with health facilities.

23. Sugar Daddy Awareness

This challenge focuses on teaching sugar daddy awareness to eighth-grade classes to reduce unwanted teenage pregnancies and HIV infections.

Applicants may explore ways to distribute an evidence-based educational intervention through:

  • Schools.
  • Teachers.
  • Youth organizations.
  • Parent engagement.
  • Peer education.
  • Community health programmes.

The intervention should be implemented in ways that are age-appropriate, culturally sensitive and aligned with relevant education and safeguarding standards.

24. Propose Your Own Intervention

D-Prize also accepts proposals for evidence-based poverty interventions that are not included on its standard challenge list.

Applicants choosing this route must identify:

  • A clear poverty-related problem.
  • An existing intervention with credible evidence.
  • The population that lacks access to the intervention.
  • The distribution gap.
  • The proposed organization’s delivery model.
  • The expected social impact.
  • The plan for piloting and scaling.

The proposed intervention should not simply be a new idea without evidence. D-Prize is specifically interested in distributing solutions that have already demonstrated effectiveness.

D-Prize Competition Timeline

The D-Prize Global Competition 2026 includes three submission deadlines.

Stage Deadline
Global Competition launches 14 September 2026
Early Submission Deadline 25 October 2026 at midnight Pacific Time
Regular Submission Deadline 15 November 2026 at midnight Pacific Time
Extension Deadline 6 December 2026 at midnight Pacific Time

Applicants who need additional time may register for an extension through the official D-Prize extension page.

Early Submission Deadline

The early submission deadline is:

25 October 2026 at midnight Pacific Time

Applicants who are ready should consider submitting early to avoid last-minute technical or preparation problems.

Regular Submission Deadline

The regular submission deadline is:

15 November 2026 at midnight Pacific Time

This is the main submission deadline listed for the competition.

Extension Deadline

The extension deadline is:

6 December 2026 at midnight Pacific Time

Applicants who require additional time should follow the official instructions for registering for an extension.

Applicants should convert the Pacific Time deadlines to their local time zones and submit well before the closing time.

D-Prize Application Process

The D-Prize selection process consists of several stages.

Round 1: Concept Note and Résumé Submission

Applicants begin by submitting:

  • A two-page concept note.
  • Résumé or résumés of the applicant or founding team.

The concept note should explain the proposed organization and distribution model. D-Prize receives more than 3,000 submissions per competition, so applicants need to communicate their ideas clearly and directly.

A strong concept note should explain:

  • Which intervention will be distributed.
  • Why the intervention matters.
  • Who lacks access to it.
  • Where the organization will operate.
  • How distribution will take place.
  • Why the applicant or team is well positioned to implement the model.
  • How the pilot will be launched.
  • How the organization could scale.
  • What the funding will make possible.

Round 2: Written Questions

The top 5% of entrepreneurs are invited to answer a set of short written questions.

Selected applicants generally have approximately two weeks to prepare and submit their responses.

At this stage, applicants may be asked to provide more detail about:

  • Their proposed intervention.
  • Their target population.
  • Their distribution strategy.
  • Their operational plan.
  • Their understanding of the local context.
  • Their team’s capabilities.
  • Their expected impact.
  • Their plans for using the seed funding.

Final Round: Interviews

Top entrepreneurs proceed to phone and email interviews.

The final stage allows D-Prize to assess the applicant’s motivation, understanding of the problem, entrepreneurial ability, proposed distribution model and readiness to launch.

Applicants should be prepared to discuss:

  • Why they selected the intervention.
  • How they will reach underserved communities.
  • What risks they anticipate.
  • How they will measure results.
  • How they will build partnerships.
  • How they will manage operations.
  • How they will use the award responsibly.
  • How they plan to raise additional funding.

Award and Launch

The top 1% of entrepreneurs receive up to US$20,000 to launch their organization.

Awardees are expected to spend the following months:

  • Piloting their distribution idea.
  • Establishing their organization.
  • Testing their operating model.
  • Reaching initial beneficiaries.
  • Measuring results.
  • Refining their approach.
  • Preparing for future growth.

The long-term goal is to build organizations that can scale their impact to reach thousands or millions of people.

How to Download the D-Prize Application Packet

Applicants should select an intervention from the official D-Prize challenge list and download the corresponding application packet.

The application packet provides information about the selected challenge and helps applicants understand the problem, intervention and expectations.

Applicants can also download the general application packet from the D-Prize website:

Download the D-Prize Application Packet

Applicants should read the relevant packet carefully before preparing their concept note.

How to Prepare a Competitive D-Prize Application

Because D-Prize receives thousands of submissions, applicants should ensure that their proposal is specific, practical and evidence-based.

1. Select the Right Intervention

Choose an intervention that:

  • Addresses a significant poverty-related need.
  • Has credible evidence of impact.
  • Is relevant to the target population.
  • Can realistically be distributed in the proposed location.
  • Matches the applicant’s skills and experience.
  • Has potential for scale.

Applicants should avoid choosing an intervention only because it sounds interesting. The proposed distribution model must be realistic within the local context.

2. Define the Distribution Gap

Explain why the intervention is not reaching enough people.

Possible barriers may include:

  • Geographic distance.
  • High costs.
  • Limited information.
  • Weak supply chains.
  • Lack of trained providers.
  • Poor community awareness.
  • Inadequate referral systems.
  • Stockouts.
  • Limited trust.
  • Weak coordination between service providers.

A strong proposal should identify the specific last-mile problem the organization intends to solve.

3. Identify the Target Population

Applicants should clearly describe who will benefit from the intervention.

This may include:

  • Low-income households.
  • Rural communities.
  • Smallholder farmers.
  • Children.
  • Pregnant women.
  • Patients with limited access to care.
  • Students in resource-limited schools.
  • Vulnerable newborns.
  • Underserved populations.
  • Communities lacking access to clean water.

The target population should be specific rather than described broadly as “everyone in need.”

4. Explain the Delivery Model

Applicants should describe exactly how the intervention will reach beneficiaries.

The proposal should answer questions such as:

  • Who will distribute the intervention?
  • Where will distribution occur?
  • How will beneficiaries be identified?
  • What partnerships are needed?
  • How will products or services be transported?
  • How will quality be maintained?
  • How will demand be generated?
  • How will the organization monitor delivery?
  • How will the model remain affordable and accessible?

5. Demonstrate Local Understanding

Applicants should show that they understand the local environment in which the organization will operate.

This may include knowledge of:

  • Local communities.
  • Existing service providers.
  • Government systems.
  • Health or education infrastructure.
  • Agricultural value chains.
  • Transport networks.
  • Cultural considerations.
  • Regulatory requirements.
  • Existing organizations working in the sector.

6. Present a Realistic Pilot Plan

The pilot should be achievable within the available funding and time.

Applicants should identify:

  • The initial geographic area.
  • The first group of beneficiaries.
  • The activities to be tested.
  • The staff or volunteers required.
  • The expected outputs.
  • The indicators that will be measured.
  • The likely risks.
  • The approach to learning and adaptation.

7. Explain the Path to Scale

D-Prize is interested in organizations that can eventually reach large numbers of people.

Applicants should explain how the organization could grow after the pilot through:

  • Additional fundraising.
  • Government partnerships.
  • Institutional partnerships.
  • Revenue generation where appropriate.
  • Replication in other locations.
  • Training and franchising.
  • Expanded distribution networks.
  • Strong monitoring and evidence.
  • Strategic partnerships.

8. Highlight Relevant Experience

Applicants should use their résumé or team résumé to demonstrate relevant skills.

Useful experience may include:

  • Entrepreneurship.
  • Project management.
  • Community engagement.
  • Public health.
  • Education.
  • Agriculture.
  • Logistics.
  • Research.
  • Monitoring and evaluation.
  • Fundraising.
  • Team leadership.
  • Product distribution.
  • Social enterprise development.

Previous experience is valuable, but applicants should focus on showing why they are capable of executing the proposed plan.

Why D-Prize Is Different from a Traditional Grant

D-Prize is different from many conventional grants because it emphasizes the creation of new organizations and the distribution of proven solutions.

Traditional grants may support established programmes, research projects, institutional activities or general organizational operations. D-Prize, by contrast, is designed primarily to support entrepreneurs who want to launch a new organization focused on delivering evidence-based interventions.

The competition emphasizes:

  • Distribution rather than invention.
  • Practical implementation rather than theory alone.
  • Early-stage entrepreneurship.
  • Measurable social impact.
  • Last-mile access.
  • Pilot testing.
  • Organizational growth.
  • Long-term scalability.

Applicants should therefore frame their proposal as an organization-building and distribution project rather than simply a research proposal or general community initiative.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Before applying, candidates should carefully consider the following:

  • The competition is primarily for new organizations.
  • The proposed intervention should be evidence-based.
  • The organization must focus on distribution or delivery.
  • The funding is seed capital, not a guaranteed long-term budget.
  • Applicants should be prepared to pilot their idea.
  • The proposed model should have potential for scale.
  • Existing organizations may face restrictions based on age and funding history.
  • Applicants should review the official eligibility rules.
  • Health-related proposals must comply with relevant laws and professional standards.
  • Applicants should submit the correct application packet for their chosen intervention.
  • All deadlines are expressed in Pacific Time.
  • The application process is highly competitive.

Official Application Links

Applicants can explore the available challenges and begin the application process through the official D-Prize website.

  • Explore D-Prize Interventions
  • Download the Application Packet
  • Read the D-Prize Frequently Asked Questions
  • Register for an Extension
  • Visit the Official D-Prize Website

Conclusion

The D-Prize Competition 2026 offers entrepreneurs and changemakers an opportunity to receive up to US$20,000 to launch organizations that distribute proven poverty solutions to underserved communities.

The competition is built on the understanding that effective interventions already exist in areas such as health, education, agriculture, water, livelihoods and public services, but many people still lack access to them. D-Prize seeks innovative distribution models that can close these gaps and deliver practical solutions to the last mile.

Applicants can choose from a wide range of intervention challenges, including childhood diarrhea treatment, maternal health, child immunization, water filters, agricultural inputs, post-harvest support, education, road safety, government transparency and poverty graduation. They may also propose their own evidence-based intervention if it is not included on the existing list.

The competition is particularly suitable for early-stage entrepreneurs and first-time founders, especially those based in low- and middle-income countries. Applicants should be able to demonstrate a clear understanding of the distribution problem, a practical delivery model, a realistic pilot plan and the potential to scale their impact.

The D-Prize Global Competition launches on 14 September 2026, with the early submission deadline on 25 October 2026, the regular deadline on 15 November 2026, and the extension deadline on 6 December 2026, all at midnight Pacific Time.

Entrepreneurs with a strong commitment to poverty reduction and the ability to distribute proven solutions are encouraged to review the challenge options, download the relevant application packet and prepare a clear, evidence-based proposal.

Discover more global Grant and Competition opportunities on OFY.

item.content:encoded:
The NATO Science for Peace and Security (SPS) Programme has opened its 2027-1 Call for Proposals, inviting scientists, experts, researchers and eligible institutions from NATO member countries and selected NATO partner countries to submit proposals addressing emerging security challenges through scientific research, technological innovation and international knowledge exchange.

The programme provides opportunities for Multi-Year Projects (MYPs) and SPS-supported scientific events, including Advanced Research Workshops, Advanced Training Courses and Advanced Study Institutes. Successful activities can receive funding, expert advice and programme support to develop practical, civil security-relevant solutions that contribute to NATO’s strategic objectives.

The 2027-1 call places particular emphasis on emerging areas such as countering unmanned systems, critical infrastructure protection, hybrid threats, energy resilience, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, and space technologies.

The deadline for full proposals is 15 November 2026 at 23:59 CET.

About the NATO Science for Peace and Security Programme

The NATO Science for Peace and Security Programme promotes dialogue and practical cooperation between NATO member states and partner countries.

Through scientific research, technological innovation and knowledge exchange, the SPS Programme brings together scientists, experts and officials to collaborate on security challenges that have implications for NATO and its partner countries.

The programme is designed to support practical, civil security-relevant activities that align with NATO’s strategic priorities. It enables researchers and experts from different countries to work together, develop innovative solutions and establish long-term professional and scientific partnerships.

Funding and support through the SPS Programme can help participating institutions conduct collaborative research, organize specialized scientific events, develop technologies and strengthen cooperation between NATO member states and eligible partner countries.

What Does the 2027-1 NATO SPS Call for Proposals Support?

For this call, the SPS Programme is accepting applications under two broad categories:

1. Multi-Year Projects

Multi-Year Projects are collaborative research and development activities designed to address security-related challenges through practical scientific and technological solutions.

Projects typically run for 24 to 36 months. Shorter implementation periods may also be considered where applicants provide adequate justification.

The programme expects project results to improve upon the existing state of the art and generally aims for results reaching Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) 3–6.

This means projects should go beyond theoretical research and demonstrate a meaningful pathway toward practical application.

2. SPS Events

The call also supports specialized scientific and expert events, including:

  • Advanced Research Workshops
  • Advanced Training Courses
  • Advanced Study Institutes

Applicants proposing events are expected to demonstrate that the activity will generate outcomes beyond simply organizing a meeting, workshop or training programme.

The proposal should explain how the event will contribute to NATO-relevant objectives and how its findings, recommendations, research outputs or other results will reach relevant stakeholders and communities of interest.

Networking can be an important part of an SPS-supported event, but networking alone cannot be the primary objective.

Key Areas of Interest for the 2027-1 Call

Applications aligned with any of the SPS Programme’s Key Priorities are welcome.

However, the 2027-1 call identifies several topics of particular interest.

Non-Kinetic Mitigation Measures Against Unmanned Systems

The programme is interested in innovative approaches to addressing security challenges associated with unmanned systems.

Applicants may explore scientific, technological or operational approaches that can help mitigate risks associated with unmanned systems without relying exclusively on conventional kinetic measures.

Protection of Critical Infrastructure, Supplies and Personnel

Another area of interest is the protection and resilience of critical infrastructure, essential supplies and personnel.

This includes particular attention to:

  • Critical infrastructure protection
  • Maritime infrastructure resilience
  • Undersea infrastructure resilience
  • Protection of essential supplies
  • Protection of personnel
  • Systems and technologies that can maintain essential functions during disruptions

Deterrence and Defence Against Hybrid Tactics

The call encourages proposals addressing hybrid security challenges.

Potential projects may focus on:

  • Technologies for addressing hybrid threats
  • New approaches to deterrence and defence
  • Cross-sector coordination
  • International cooperation
  • Technologies and systems that strengthen resilience against hybrid tactics

Innovative Energy Generation, Storage and Distribution

Energy resilience is another priority area.

The programme is particularly interested in innovative approaches to energy generation, storage and distribution, including technologies and systems that enable critical facilities and deployed systems to continue operating during prolonged interruptions to energy supplies.

Projects may therefore address the resilience of energy systems and the ability of critical infrastructure to function despite extended disruptions.

Biotechnology and Artificial Intelligence

The call identifies biotechnology as an area of particular interest, including the convergence between biotechnology and artificial intelligence.

Researchers and experts working at the intersection of biotechnology and AI may therefore find opportunities to develop collaborative projects addressing relevant security challenges.

Space Technologies

Space-related technologies are also highlighted.

Topics of interest include:

  • Space awareness
  • Positioning
  • Navigation
  • Timing
  • Technologies supporting resilient space-enabled capabilities

Applicants working on innovative space technologies with clear links to security objectives may consider the SPS Programme as a potential source of collaborative research and development support.

Who Can Apply?

The NATO SPS Programme has specific eligibility requirements.

Applicants must meet all applicable eligibility criteria to have their proposals considered.

A proposal must:

  1. Contribute to NATO’s strategic objectives and have a clear connection to security.
  2. Address at least one of the SPS Key Priorities.
  3. Be jointly developed by scientists or experts from at least one NATO member country and at least one eligible NATO partner country.
  4. Include the required NATO and partner-country Project Directors.
  5. Be developed and implemented by eligible institutions.
  6. Include realistic plans and budgets.
  7. Follow the rules and regulations contained in the relevant SPS handbooks.

Required Project Directors

Each proposed activity must include two key leadership roles.

NATO Country Project Director

The activity must include a NATO country Project Director (NPD).

The NPD must:

  • Be a scientist or expert;
  • Be a resident in a NATO member country; and
  • Be employed in a NATO member country.

Partner Country Project Director

The activity must also include a Partner country Project Director (PPD).

The PPD must:

  • Be a scientist or expert;
  • Be a resident in an eligible NATO partner country; and
  • Be employed in an eligible NATO partner country.

For Multi-Year Projects, additional Co-Directors from NATO member countries or eligible partner countries may also participate.

Eligible Institutions

Projects must be developed and implemented by Co-Directors who are employed by eligible organizations.

These include:

  • Governmental institutions
  • Academic institutions
  • Other non-profit institutions

For-profit private companies are not eligible for SPS funding.

This institutional requirement is particularly important for applicants considering participation through private-sector organizations. A proposal involving a for-profit private company as the institution responsible for the SPS-funded activity would not meet the stated eligibility requirements.

Eligible Countries

The programme allows participation from specified NATO member countries and eligible NATO partner countries.

NATO Member Countries

Eligible NATO member countries include:

  • Albania
  • Belgium
  • Bulgaria
  • Canada
  • Croatia
  • Czechia
  • Denmark
  • Estonia
  • Finland
  • France
  • Germany
  • Greece
  • Hungary

  • Lithuania

  • Norway

  • Türkiye
  • United Kingdom
  • United States of America

Eligible NATO Partner Countries

Eligible NATO partner countries include:

  • Algeria
  • Armenia
  • Australia
  • Austria
  • Azerbaijan
  • Bahrain
  • Bosnia and Herzegovina
  • Colombia

  • Tajikistan

  • Ukraine
  • United Arab Emirates
  • Uzbekistan

Important: Ghana is not included in the eligible NATO member or NATO partner country lists provided in this call. Therefore, individuals and institutions based in Ghana would not be eligible to participate as the required country Project Director or participating institution under this specific call unless their circumstances otherwise satisfy the programme’s country eligibility rules.

Funding Available Under Multi-Year Projects

The NATO SPS Programme does not establish a strict maximum budget for Multi-Year Projects.

However, the call states that budgets for projects lasting 36 months are typically around €400,000.

Higher budgets may be considered where they are adequately justified, particularly for:

  • Activities aligned with priority deliverables; and
  • Proposals involving large consortia of institutions.

Applicants should therefore develop budgets based on the actual work required to achieve the proposed results rather than simply attempting to request the largest possible amount.

Co-Financing

Applicants may choose to use co-financing.

The call indicates that a reasonable amount of co-financing is up to one-third of the total grant amount.

SPS may consider higher levels of co-financing on a case-by-case basis where the proposal provides sufficient justification.

Project Duration

The typical duration of an SPS Multi-Year Project is:

24 to 36 months

Shorter projects may be considered if the applicant provides a convincing justification.

Applicants should also account for anticipated procurement timelines when developing the project schedule.

This is important because procurement and other administrative processes can affect the actual time required to deliver a project.

What Makes a Strong SPS Proposal?

Applicants are encouraged to thoroughly research the existing state of the art before submitting their proposal.

A strong application should demonstrate:

  • Awareness of existing academic research;
  • Awareness of relevant industrial developments;
  • Understanding of current technologies and approaches;
  • A clear explanation of what is innovative about the proposed activity;
  • Evidence that the proposed work differs from existing work;
  • Appropriate and recent literature references;
  • A realistic implementation plan;
  • A realistic budget;
  • Clear security relevance;
  • Alignment with NATO strategic objectives; and
  • A credible pathway toward practical results.

Applicants should clearly explain how their proposed work improves upon or differs from existing efforts.

The state-of-the-art analysis does not necessarily need to become the main objective of the activity. Instead, it should demonstrate that the applicants understand the existing research and technology landscape and can clearly identify the contribution of their proposed work.

Technology Readiness Levels

For Multi-Year Projects, the SPS Programme expects project results to aim for Technology Readiness Levels 3–6.

Applicants should therefore consider how their research can progress toward practical technological development rather than remaining entirely theoretical.

Projects should demonstrate how the proposed work can improve the state of the art, including where relevant through improvements over commercially available off-the-shelf solutions.

Requirements for Multi-Year Project Applications

A complete Multi-Year Project proposal must include the application submitted through the SPS grant platform along with the required supporting documentation.

Applicants should prepare:

  • A completed SPS application form;
  • A project schedule, such as a Gantt chart or another suitable project timeline;
  • An end-user commitment letter for each project end-user;
  • A brief overview of participating institutions;
  • SPS MYP Detailed Budget in the required Excel format;
  • SPS MYP Acceptance of Funds;
  • SPS MYP Agreement for Joint Research; and
  • An SPS MYP Sample Intellectual Property Rights Agreement or an IPR waiver agreed upon by all participants and their institutions.

These documents form an important part of a complete application.

Requirements for SPS Events

For Events, applicants must submit a complete application through the SPS grant platform together with the required supporting documentation.

The required documents include:

  • SPS Events Budget;
  • SPS Events Acceptance of Funds; and
  • SPS Events Cooperation Agreement.

Applicants should also clearly explain the purpose of the event, its relevance to NATO and its expected impact on relevant stakeholders and communities of interest.

How to Apply for the NATO SPS 2027-1 Call

Applications must be submitted through the official NATO SPS grant platform.

Proposals submitted through other means, including email, will not be considered. Read the full proposal HERE

Step 1: Register

Applicants should first create an account on the SPS grant platform.

Step 2: Find the Opportunity

After registering, applicants should identify the relevant available opportunity on the platform homepage.

Step 3: Start the Application

Applicants should select “Start application” and choose the appropriate grant mechanism.

This may be a Multi-Year Project or an eligible SPS Event.

Step 4: Complete the Proposal

Applicants should provide all required information and upload the relevant supporting documents.

Step 5: Review the Application

Before submission, applicants should carefully check that:

  • All required fields have been completed;
  • The correct grant mechanism has been selected;
  • All supporting documents have been included;
  • The project budget is realistic;
  • The project schedule is achievable;
  • The proposal demonstrates security relevance;
  • The proposal addresses an SPS Key Priority;
  • The required NATO and partner-country Project Directors are included; and
  • The participating countries and institutions meet eligibility requirements.

Step 6: Submit Before the Deadline

Applicants are strongly advised not to wait until the final hours to submit their proposals.

The programme specifically advises applicants against last-minute submissions.

Proposal Evaluation Process

After submission, proposals undergo an evaluation process.

The proposal will be evaluated by the SPS Office and the Independent Scientific Evaluation Group (ISEG).

Proposals recommended for funding by the ISEG are then shared with the NATO Partnerships and Cooperative Security Committee (PCSC) for approval.

Applicants should therefore expect a detailed review process rather than an immediate funding decision.

How Long Does the Evaluation Take?

The SPS Programme states that a funding decision can take up to nine months following an application deadline.

Applicants should take this timeframe into account when proposing dates for their projects or events.

This is particularly important for events because applicants should avoid proposing an activity date that would occur before sufficient time has been allowed for the review and funding process.

Important Rules on Multiple Submissions

There are restrictions on the number of proposals an individual can lead.

Co-Directors are limited to one proposal per call.

This means that an individual cannot serve as Co-Director on multiple proposals under the same call.

Rules for Ongoing SPS Activities

Applicants who are already directing an SPS activity must ensure that the existing activity has been formally closed before applying as a Co-Director for a new activity.

A person cannot simultaneously serve as Co-Director of multiple activities.

However, Co-Directors of ongoing activities may participate in new proposals as participants, provided that doing so does not interfere with their existing work.

Budget Planning

Applicants should ensure that proposed budgets are balanced and realistic.

The call specifically states that each Co-Director’s institution should receive an appropriate portion of the project budget.

Applicants should therefore make sure that the budget reflects the actual responsibilities, activities, resources and contributions of participating institutions.

A strong budget should be closely connected to the proposed work plan and should provide a reasonable justification for major expenses.

Intellectual Property Considerations

Multi-Year Project applicants must address intellectual property rights as part of the application.

The proposal must include either:

  • An SPS MYP Sample Intellectual Property Rights Agreement; or
  • An IPR waiver agreed upon by all participants and their institutions.

This ensures that participating institutions understand and agree on how intellectual property arising from the collaborative research will be handled.

End-User Participation

Multi-Year Projects must include an end-user commitment letter for each project end-user.

This requirement emphasizes the practical orientation of SPS-supported projects.

Applicants should therefore consider who will ultimately use, implement or benefit from the project’s results and demonstrate meaningful engagement with those end-users.

Diversity and Inclusion

The NATO SPS Programme states that it is committed to diversity and inclusion.

Eligible applicants are welcomed regardless of:

  • Gender
  • Age
  • Nationality
  • Ethnicity
  • Religion or belief
  • Cultural background
  • Sexual orientation
  • Disability

However, applicants must still meet the programme’s specific country, institutional and project eligibility requirements.

Deadline for the NATO SPS 2027-1 Call for Proposals

The deadline for submitting full proposals is:

15 November 2026 at 23:59 CET

Applications must be submitted through the SPS grant platform before the deadline.

The call warns that data relating to incomplete applications will be lost after the deadline.

Applicants are therefore strongly encouraged to submit their proposals well before the closing time.

Where to Get More Information

Applicants should familiarize themselves with the relevant SPS documentation before preparing their proposals.

In particular, applicants are encouraged to review:

  • The SPS Events Handbook;
  • The SPS Multi-Year Project Handbook;
  • SPS grant application templates;
  • SPS budget documents;
  • SPS acceptance of funds documents;
  • SPS cooperation and joint research agreements; and
  • Guidance on managing SPS grants.

The official NATO SPS resources provide further information on the programme and the management of SPS-supported activities.

Applicants with questions before submitting an application should direct their enquiries to the SPS Programme through the contact form provided on the NATO SPS website.

Key Takeaways

The NATO Science for Peace and Security 2027-1 Call for Proposals provides an opportunity for eligible scientists, experts and institutions to collaborate internationally on practical security-related scientific and technological challenges.

The most important points to remember are:

  • The programme supports Multi-Year Projects and Events.
  • Multi-Year Projects typically run for 24–36 months.
  • Typical funding for a 36-month Multi-Year Project is around €400,000, although there is no fixed hard budget limit.
  • Higher budgets may be considered where properly justified.
  • Projects should generally target Technology Readiness Levels 3–6.
  • Proposals must have a clear connection to security and NATO strategic objectives.
  • Proposals must address at least one SPS Key Priority.
  • Projects must involve eligible participants from at least one NATO member country and one eligible NATO partner country.
  • A NATO country Project Director and Partner country Project Director are required.
  • Co-Directors must work for governmental, academic or other non-profit institutions.
  • For-profit private companies are not eligible for SPS funding.
  • Applicants must submit through the official SPS grant platform.
  • Proposals submitted by email or other methods will not be accepted.
  • Co-Directors may submit or lead only one proposal per call.
  • The funding decision process can take up to nine months after the deadline.
  • The full proposal deadline is 15 November 2026 at 23:59 CET.

Conclusion

The NATO Science for Peace and Security 2027-1 Call for Proposals offers a significant opportunity for eligible researchers, scientists, experts and non-profit institutions to develop international collaborations addressing some of the most important emerging security challenges.

The call is particularly relevant to researchers and institutions working in areas such as unmanned systems, critical infrastructure resilience, hybrid threats, energy security, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, and space technologies.

However, eligibility is highly structured. Applicants must establish a qualifying partnership between a NATO member country and an eligible NATO partner country, appoint the required Project Directors, work through an eligible institution and demonstrate a clear connection between the proposed activity and NATO’s strategic security objectives.

Potential applicants should begin developing their partnerships, research concept, project schedule, budget and supporting documentation well before the deadline. Given the detailed evaluation process and the possibility of decisions taking up to nine months, applicants should also plan their proposed project or event dates carefully.

Deadline: 15 November 2026 at 23:59 CET.

All proposals must be submitted through the designated NATO SPS grant platform before the deadline.

item.content:encoded:
Aidsfonds has announced the upcoming launch of the ActHIVate Fund Request for Proposals, a new funding opportunity designed to strengthen community-led HIV responses for men who have sex with men (MSM) and trans communities in countries and settings where access to healthcare remains highly restricted.

With a total of €2 million available in the first funding round, the ActHIVate Fund will provide flexible support to established MSM- and trans-led community organisations delivering HIV-related healthcare, conducting strategic advocacy, and working to integrate inclusive services into existing health systems.

The first full Request for Proposals is scheduled to open on 21 September 2026, with applications due by 25 October 2026.

The funding will cover an implementation period of approximately one year and nine months, from April 2027 to December 2028, and Aidsfonds expects to award funding to up to 20 organisations.

About the ActHIVate Fund

The ActHIVate Fund has been developed in response to increasing challenges faced by community-led organisations working with MSM and trans communities.

MSM and trans people continue to experience disproportionately high levels of HIV infection in many parts of the world. At the same time, they can face significant barriers when attempting to access healthcare, including stigma, discrimination, criminalisation, hostile political environments and limited availability of inclusive health services.

For many years, community-led organisations and peer outreach initiatives have played a critical role in addressing these challenges. These organisations have helped communities access HIV prevention, testing, treatment linkages, follow-up support and other essential health services while also advocating for human rights and more inclusive healthcare systems.

However, the organisations providing these services are increasingly operating under financial and political pressure.

The ActHIVate Fund has therefore been created to provide flexible and accessible funding to organisations that are already doing this critical work and need resources to maintain services, strengthen their organisations and advocate for sustainable changes within health systems.

Why the ActHIVate Fund Is Needed

The global HIV response has entered a challenging period as international development funding has declined and several major funding streams have experienced significant disruptions.

According to information provided by Aidsfonds, official development assistance from OECD Development Assistance Committee members decreased by 23.1%, representing the largest single-year decline recorded.

Funding disruptions have also had a direct effect on HIV services.

Cuts and changes affecting PEPFAR-supported programmes have particularly affected prevention and community-based HIV services. Aidsfonds cites findings from amfAR’s PEPFAR Pulse Study indicating that prevention investment declined sharply, with 51% less funding available and 43% of service providers forced to stop providing at least one prevention service.

The funding crisis has also contributed to the closure of health facilities and the discontinuation of HIV programme components. According to Aidsfonds, at least 1,700 health facilities have closed, while 73% of service providers have discontinued at least one component of their HIV programmes.

These changes can disproportionately affect key populations, including MSM and trans people, who may already experience significant difficulties accessing mainstream health services.

The ActHIVate Fund seeks to help address this situation by supporting organisations that are embedded within the affected communities and have the experience and relationships necessary to provide services effectively.

Objective of the ActHIVate Fund

The central objective of ActHIVate is to support community-led HIV responses for MSM and trans communities in restrictive and criminalised environments.

The fund will focus on three major areas:

  1. Community-led HIV-related healthcare service delivery
  2. Strategic advocacy
  3. Integration of MSM- and trans-friendly services into existing health systems

The programme is not intended simply to provide short-term emergency funding.

Instead, it aims to support organisations in addressing immediate health needs while also generating evidence and strengthening approaches that can influence healthcare systems over the longer term.

Successful applicants are therefore expected to demonstrate how their community-led work can contribute to stronger, more inclusive and sustainable HIV and healthcare responses.

How the ActHIVate Fund Was Developed

The fund was developed through extensive consultations with representatives of MSM and trans communities.

These consultations highlighted the urgent need for funding that is:

  • Flexible
  • Accessible
  • Responsive to community needs
  • Capable of sustaining essential HIV-related services
  • Supportive of advocacy and human rights efforts
  • Suitable for organisations working in difficult or restrictive environments

Community representatives emphasised that organisations already working within these communities understand their needs and are often best positioned to deliver effective services.

As a result, ActHIVate places community organisations at the centre of both implementation and decision-making.

What Activities Can the ActHIVate Grant Support?

The ActHIVate Fund has a broad scope covering HIV services, advocacy and organisational strengthening.

1. Community-Led HIV Service Delivery

Funding can support community-led HIV-related healthcare services, including:

  • HIV prevention
  • Linkages to HIV treatment
  • Follow-up support
  • Other allied health services that are particularly important to MSM and trans communities in the applicant’s context

Applicants should demonstrate a clear understanding of the health needs of the communities they serve and explain how their proposed activities will address barriers to accessing appropriate services.

2. Building Evidence for Advocacy

Organisations can use their service-delivery experience to build evidence that can strengthen their advocacy efforts.

This may involve documenting:

  • Service gaps
  • Community healthcare needs
  • Barriers to accessing healthcare
  • Experiences of MSM and trans communities
  • Lessons learned from community-led service delivery

The evidence generated should contribute to advocacy for policy and health-system improvements.

3. Advocacy for Better Healthcare Access

The fund can support advocacy aimed at reducing barriers preventing MSM and trans communities from accessing HIV and other essential health services.

This may include efforts to:

  • Promote more inclusive healthcare policies
  • Address discriminatory barriers
  • Improve access to HIV services
  • Advocate for more responsive healthcare systems
  • Strengthen recognition of the healthcare needs of MSM and trans communities

4. Integration of Inclusive Services Into Health Systems

Another important area of ActHIVate is advocacy for better integration of MSM- and trans-friendly services into existing healthcare systems and policies.

The long-term objective is to demonstrate approaches that can influence and strengthen mainstream health responses rather than operating entirely outside existing systems.

5. Organisational Core Strengthening

ActHIVate recognises that organisations require more than project-specific funding to remain effective.

The fund can therefore provide support for core organisational strengthening, enabling organisations to build their capacity to undertake critical HIV service delivery and advocacy work.

This flexible approach recognises that strong community organisations require adequate organisational resources to sustain their work and respond effectively to changing circumstances.

Intersectionality and Other Key Populations

ActHIVate recognises that MSM and trans communities are not homogeneous groups and that individuals may experience multiple vulnerabilities simultaneously.

The fund specifically recognises the intersection between MSM and trans communities and other key populations.

For example, proposed work may take into account the experiences of:

  • MSM and trans people who are sex workers
  • MSM and trans people who use drugs
  • Other community members facing overlapping barriers to HIV prevention, treatment and healthcare

Applicants should consider the realities of the communities they serve and demonstrate how their proposed work responds to the specific context in which they operate.

Activities That Are Outside the Scope of the Fund

Although the ActHIVate Fund covers a range of HIV, advocacy and organisational activities, certain activities are specifically excluded.

Multi-Country or Regional Projects

The fund does not support multi-country or regional projects that engage more than one country.

The grant is intended to support work within the individual country of implementation described in the application.

Large-Scale Health-System Improvements

The fund does not cover large-scale health-system infrastructure or technology projects such as:

  • Establishing health information technology systems
  • Clinical software
  • Digital databases
  • Laboratory systems
  • Projects exclusively focused on community-led monitoring
  • Managing or building supply chains
  • Facilitating task shifting

Procurement of Health Products

Grant funding cannot be used for the procurement of:

  • Medicines
  • Vaccines
  • PrEP
  • ART

Applicants should ensure that their proposed budgets do not rely on the grant to purchase these products.

Conference Attendance and Hosting

The fund does not support:

  • Attendance at conferences
  • Hosting conferences

Large Capital Purchases

Large capital expenditures are outside the scope of the fund.

Examples include:

  • Buildings
  • Large equipment
  • Facilities

Research Without a Clear Advocacy or Service-Delivery Purpose

Research activities are not eligible where they do not have a clear connection to either:

  • Advocacy
  • Service delivery

Applicants should demonstrate how any research-related component directly contributes to their HIV services or advocacy objectives.

Who Can Apply for the ActHIVate Fund?

The primary applicants are registered local community organisations led by MSM and trans community members.

Organisations must have substantial demonstrated experience in relevant areas.

Eligible organisations should be able to demonstrate experience in:

  • Providing critical HIV services to MSM and trans communities
  • Conducting advocacy relating to MSM and trans health and rights
  • Engaging with local and/or national governments
  • Engaging with health systems
  • Addressing healthcare barriers affecting MSM and trans communities

Can Unregistered Organisations Apply?

Yes.

Unregistered organisations can also apply if they already have an established fiscal host.

This provides an opportunity for community organisations that may not have formal legal registration but have an appropriate fiscal-hosting arrangement in place.

Applicants should carefully review the full Request for Proposals once it is released because the complete eligibility criteria and detailed requirements will be provided at that stage.

Eligible Countries and Regions

The first ActHIVate Fund call will support organisations operating in:

Uganda

Ugandan community-led organisations meeting the programme’s requirements can apply.

Nigeria

Nigerian MSM- and trans-led community organisations that meet the eligibility requirements can also apply.

Eastern Europe and Central Asia

The fund will cover selected countries in the Eastern Europe and Central Asia (EECA) region.

The specific eligible countries should be confirmed in the full Request for Proposals.

Southwest Asia and North Africa

The fund will also operate in selected countries in the Southwest Asia and North Africa (SWANA) region.

Applicants should consult the full RFP when it is released for the definitive country list.

Important Country Restriction

The grant supports work within one country of implementation.

Multi-country or regional projects involving more than one country are outside the scope of this funding opportunity.

How Much Funding Is Available?

The first ActHIVate Fund Request for Proposals has a total funding envelope of:

€2,000,000

The funding will cover an implementation period running from:

April 2027 to December 2028

This represents approximately one year and nine months of implementation.

Aidsfonds expects that up to 20 applications will receive funding.

The exact amount available to each successful organisation and the detailed budget requirements will be specified in the full Request for Proposals.

Community-Led Decision-Making

A significant feature of the ActHIVate Fund is its approach to decision-making.

Aidsfonds states that communities should play a central role in decisions about funding and investment because community members have direct knowledge of the challenges they face and the approaches that work in their contexts.

Grant decisions will therefore be made by an ActHIVate Grantmaking Committee.

The committee will consist of external members who are community leaders and experts from the regions and communities covered by the Request for Proposals.

The aim is to develop a balanced portfolio of funded organisations based on factors such as:

  • Objectives
  • Countries and regions
  • Populations
  • Budgets

This community-centred approach is intended to ensure that funding decisions reflect the realities and priorities of the communities the programme seeks to support.

ActHIVate Fund Application Timeline

Applicants should take note of the following important dates:

Application Stage Date
Full Request for Proposals published and grants portal opens 21 September 2026
Full proposal submission deadline 25 October 2026
Funding decision Mid-December 2026
Implementation begins March/April 2027
Funding period April 2027 – December 2028

Application Deadline

The deadline for submitting the full proposal is:

25 October 2026

Organisations interested in applying should begin preparing early rather than waiting until the application portal opens.

Visit the official website HERE

Click HERE for more global grant opportunities

What Should Potential Applicants Prepare?

Because the complete RFP has not yet been released, applicants should wait for the official requirements before finalising their applications.

However, based on the announced scope of the fund, prospective applicants can begin organising information about the following areas.

1. Organisational Information

Applicants can prepare information about:

  • Registration status
  • Leadership structure
  • Community ownership and leadership
  • Fiscal host arrangements, where applicable
  • Organisational experience and capacity

2. Previous Experience

Applicants should be prepared to demonstrate previous experience in:

  • HIV service-delivery programmes
  • Prevention activities
  • Treatment linkages
  • Follow-up services
  • Advocacy initiatives
  • Government engagement
  • Health-system engagement

3. Communities Served

Applicants should clearly understand and be able to describe:

  • The MSM communities they serve
  • The trans communities they serve
  • Intersectional populations within their communities
  • Specific healthcare barriers in their local context

4. Proposed Activities

Applicants should consider how their proposed project will address relevant areas such as:

  • HIV service delivery
  • Strategic advocacy
  • Evidence generation linked to advocacy or services
  • Integration of inclusive services into health systems
  • Organisational strengthening

5. Expected Impact

Applicants should consider how their proposed project will:

  • Improve access to healthcare
  • Strengthen community-led HIV responses
  • Generate useful evidence for advocacy
  • Reduce barriers to HIV and health services
  • Improve integration of inclusive services into health systems
  • Contribute to longer-term health-system change

6. Budget Planning

Applicants should prepare realistic budgets covering eligible activities and organisational strengthening needs while ensuring that proposed expenditures comply with the fund’s restrictions.

Applicants should ensure that their plans do not include activities specifically listed as out of scope.

Q&A Session

Aidsfonds has indicated that a Q&A session will become available only after the full Request for Proposals is published.

Organisations with questions about detailed eligibility requirements, budgets, application procedures or other technical aspects should consult the full RFP and accompanying Q&A materials once they are released.

Why This Grant Opportunity Matters

The ActHIVate Fund represents an important funding opportunity for community-led organisations working at the intersection of HIV, healthcare access and human rights.

MSM and trans-led organisations often have direct relationships with communities that mainstream healthcare systems struggle to reach. Their peer-led approaches can help individuals overcome stigma, discrimination, fear and other barriers that may prevent them from seeking HIV prevention, testing, treatment or other health services.

At the same time, these organisations are operating in an increasingly difficult funding environment.

By providing flexible funding that combines service delivery, advocacy and organisational strengthening, ActHIVate aims to support organisations not only in responding to immediate healthcare needs but also in building stronger systems for the future.

Conclusion

The ActHIVate Fund is a major new grant opportunity from Aidsfonds designed to strengthen HIV responses led by and for MSM and trans communities in restrictive and criminalised settings.

With €2 million available in the first funding round, the fund will support up to 20 organisations working in Uganda, Nigeria and selected countries in Eastern Europe and Central Asia and Southwest Asia and North Africa.

The programme places particular emphasis on three interconnected areas: community-led HIV service delivery, strategic advocacy, and the integration of MSM- and trans-friendly services into existing health systems. It also provides support for organisational core strengthening, recognising that sustainable community-led responses require strong organisations and flexible resources.

Eligible organisations should have substantial experience serving MSM and trans communities, delivering HIV-related services, conducting advocacy and engaging with governments or health systems. Unregistered organisations may also be eligible where they have an established fiscal host.

The full Request for Proposals and grants portal are scheduled to open on 21 September 2026, while the full proposal submission deadline is 25 October 2026.

Prospective applicants should use the period before the launch to review their organisational experience, proposed activities, evidence, partnerships and budgets so they are prepared to respond when the complete requirements become available.

The ActHIVate Fund ultimately seeks to ensure that community-led organisations have the resources needed to continue providing essential HIV services today while helping create more inclusive and sustainable healthcare systems for MSM and trans communities in the future.
